title: Derivation of the Boltzmann equation with no "molecular chaos"-type approximation
abstract: The paper resolves the problem of the derivation of a completely closed evolution equation for $s$-particle distribution function $F_s(t)$ ($s \le N$) from the Liouville equation for $N \gg 1$-particle distribution function $F_N(t)$ with arbitrary initial condition $F_N(0)$ and without any use of the "molecular chaos" type approximation. The initial correlations are accounted for in this equation in the kernel governing the evolution of $F_s(t)$ via the special projection operator which exactly transforms the inhomogeneous Nakajima-Zwanzig Generalized Master Equation (GME) with an irrelevant initial condition term into the homogenous one. This equation is further simplified by presenting its kernel in the linear in the particles' density $n$ approximation. In this approximation the equations for one-particle $F_1(t)$ and two-particle $F_2(t)$ distribution functions are derived. It is shown that the terms describing the influence of initial correlations in the equation for $F_1(t)$ disappear at the large timescale $t \sim t_{\text{rel}} \gg t_{\text{cor}}$ ($t_{\text{cor}}$ is a short correlation time as compared to a relaxation time $t_{\text{rel}}$ of $F_1(t)$) resulting in the linear Boltzmann equation. This equation can be presented as the nonlinear Boltzmann equation in the time interval $t_{\text{cor}} \ll t \ll t_{\text{rel}}$. At $t_{\text{rel}} \to \infty$ (mean free path $l \to \infty$) the Boltzmann equation holds for all finite times $t \gg t_{\text{cor}}$.
summary: This paper presents a sophisticated derivation of kinetic evolution equations, such as the Boltzmann equation, directly from the full Liouville dynamics of interacting particles. By employing a specialized projection operator formalism, it overcomes the limitations of previous methods that required assuming molecular chaos or ignoring initial correlations. The result confirms the validity of the Boltzmann description in appropriate time limits while maintaining mathematical rigor regarding initial state preparation.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of deriving a closed evolution equation for reduced $s$-particle distribution functions from the full Liouville equation without invoking the 'molecular chaos' approximation.
main_result: It rigorously derives that in the long-time limit ($t \gg t_{	ext{cor}}$), the system approaches the linear Boltzmann equation, and in an intermediate regime, it matches the nonlinear Boltzmann equation, all while correctly accounting for initial correlations.
method: The derivation employs a specialized projection operator formalism applied to the Nakajima-Zwanzig Generalized Master Equation (GME) to transform the inhomogeneous GME into an exact, homogeneous form.
model_or_system: The system consists of $N$ interacting classical particles governed by the Liouville equation. The analysis focuses on deriving equations for reduced density functions ($F_s$) describing subsystems of $s$ particles coupled to a large environment ($\Sigma$).
key_observables: Reduced distribution functions $F_s(t)$, particularly $F_1(t)$ and $F_2(t)$; the collision integral $J$.
important_parameters: Time scales: correlation time ($t_{	ext{cor}}$), relaxation time ($t_{	ext{rel}}$); Density parameter ($\gamma$); Mean free path ($l$).
main_assumptions: The derivation relies on a small density approximation ($\gamma \ll 1$) and the assumption that initial correlations can be systematically incorporated into the evolution kernel.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the need for an exact, closed GME using projection operators. It then derives the time-convolution form of the equation, showing how initial correlation terms are managed. Finally, it analyzes the long-time limit to recover the standard Boltzmann equation forms.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous theoretical framework for deriving kinetic equations like the Boltzmann equation from first principles (Liouville dynamics) while correctly handling non-equilibrium initial conditions and avoiding common approximations used in statistical mechanics.
